blocks.x: You can get your name first, your full name.
My name is Edward Thomas Johnson.

Edward Thomas. Thomas Johnson. And I mentioned that we're doing this over on 934 Royal, not Royal, Bourbon Street, at the Ralph Collins Place, who's here. This is Bill Russell. And we would like to ask just when you were born and where?
I'm born 1903, August 24th, in New Orleans, Louisiana.
1903, right here. What part of town?
In the third one. On Ivoryville between Dorevny and Rowan.
Did any of your folks play music? Your father, mother, any uncles or anybody else in the family play music when you were young?
No, not that I know of.
What did you get started? What instrument did you start on?
Well, I first started on a ukulele.
How old were you about?
I was about 14 then.
Did you ever have any lessons on any of those instruments that you took up or just pick everything up yourself?
Oh, I just picked it up myself. A boyfriend of mine by the name of Daniel Steard, he's now in California.
Can you remember the first music you ever heard around town? Either dance bands or the streets on the brass bands? What was the first music you could remember hearing when you were a kid?
Well, when I was a kid I was going to Biennale School. I used to remember when they have those funerals, the manual parades and all them old musicians used to play.
When did you take up your tuba?
I took a bass tuba around 1945.

In late years then you took that one. Yes, right. What else did you take after you learned your ukulele? Did you play with any bands with that or any groups you know? I mean, any other kids around? What kind of a group did you play with or by yourself?

Oh yes, in 1924 I was staying on 1809 Biennale Street, that's Biennale, near Duhiven. And they had a big boarding house next to where I was. And the whole time, the brass bands, well I wouldn't know if the people paid their rent or not, but they put them out. And they left the old band in there. And we kids was out there playing around in the place and we took the old band post loose. Because we used to sell that brass for junk. And I'd blow through a part of it and it sounded like a bass. And then I took two pieces and put together and made it slide. And then they used to have these old time graphenola horns, round records, I believe it was Edison. Used to have a little bit of a little bit of a black horn with a brass tip. And I sold that onto the end of that brass bed.

Is it bigger than the Persia Victor horn? Is it bigger than this? I mean smaller? Just about a little smaller. A little smaller than this is a standard Victor horn with the brass on the end. Yeah, it's a little smaller. It must have been from a little cellular machine like on the Edison or Columbia, they had little tiny ones too. You put that on the answer.

I made a horn out of it. And I blowed it and by moving up and down I could make chords. Yeah. And there was a fellow by the name of Walter Nelson, he played a guitar. And another fellow by the name of Joseph Pierre. And another fellow by the name of Samuel Dominic, we used to call him Bebe. He's in California, he has a stroke now, he don't play anymore. Joseph Pierre, he don't play anymore. He's in Biloxi, Mississippi. And we used to go around town. And we used to name that the Funnel Foam. The Funnel Foam? The Funnel Foam. And there was a fellow staying on Boi Bun and St. Peter. His name was Walter Coquille. But he used to go by the name of Ma'er Pompom from Bayou Pompom. And he picked us up around 19, by the last part of 1924. And he brought us to Edgewater Gulf Hotel in Biloxi, Mississippi. On the Shells Convention. And that's where we met this fellow with a hillbilly man called Bob Burns. Oh yeah. And that's when he-
Was he on radio then already? Was he on radio? I used to hear him on radio when I was younger.

He said, oh you didn't hear no talk of him. He wasn't known then. Wasn't thanks. Or nothing like that until 29. After he saw my horn. And in 1929, in 28, then you begin to hear talk of Bob Burns and Ben Crosby. And he named the horn the bazooka. So after everybody saw me play that, they started calling it bazooka so I wouldn't tell them no better.
So you still call it the bazooka then? It's still called the bazooka.

But you called the funnel foam? That was the first that we gave them. Did you have any mouthpiece on there? No, there was a piece of brass. One of them old brass unions at that time. Oh yeah, so you just blew into that. And we put that, I saw that on there, and put that over it so it wouldn't make, the brass would make your mouth so. Yeah. How did you- I have the old one on there. Did you start to sing into that?
No, you blow. You blow it and make it the sound of a bass tuba. Just like you do on a tuba? You don't really sing in it then?
No, you don't sing.
I thought maybe you were singing in that. You got your lips just vibrating in like it sings on a tuba.
Yeah, it's small, most of those lips wake in the sly.
Yeah, I wondered. I thought maybe you were just singing into that. Like they do on the little kazoo's, you know, you started singing to that.
Oh no, you don't sing in that.
Yeah, I see. Well where else did you go? How long did you stay over there at the-

Oh, we used to go over there with male, we call them male pom pom, where we'd go for the weekend events. Just go for a weekend. We used to stay out in the dormitory. And we played several other places.
How many were in the group? About three or four?
At that time there was four of us. Four.
What other instruments did you have in that band?
Well they had two guitars and two little kazoo horns.
Oh, kazoo?
Yeah. So I had one made like a trumpet.
And your kazooca? Well that'd be actually five pieces. No, four. Two guitars you say?
Two guitars, myself and others.
Oh, I remember. Just a water kazoo. How long did you play together?
Oh, we played together for about eight or nine years.
Well, did you pick up the- when did you pick up the guitar?
Well Walter Nelson learned me the guitar.
Well that was after you'd been playing the bazooka?
Oh yeah, yeah, yeah.
About what year would that be?
Huh?
About what year was that?
Oh, it must have been somewhere around about 26, 27.
While you were playing with that group.
Oh yeah, yeah.
Did you travel anyplace else after that, besides the Biloxi Hotel?

Oh yeah, we went to Nashville, Tennessee, with a fellow called Steve Devoidy. He was a sailman for the Tennessee and Animal Company. And we played at the Belle Mique Club over there. What player did you play?
What player did you play?
In a lot of places. I just can't recall.

When you played with you in that group, did you ever play for any regular dances or was it just mostly as an entertainment? Entertainment, it was entertainment. Did you travel with any shows at any time? I've heard you were traveling at some times at shows, did you? No, we played. Any Kent shows or anything like that? No, we played amateur in the theater's palace. Oh, you played around?
Yeah, Win First Pride.
Yeah, here in town. Yeah. How late did that Palace Theater run that you played for it? They had shows, I mean that way.
Oh, let's see, but here I think it was around 39, something 40 I believe when they stopped in the water.
Back about the time the war started then? Yeah. Did you ever play any shows like that at the old Lyric? Did they have anything there?
Yeah, but we never had a chance. You never did play that?

Yeah, yeah. That's where they had Robichur's band, wasn't it? They had a regular band there. Did you ever play any dances anyplace? That is, was this music suitable for dancing to you? I mean did you actually play for dances someplace?

Well we had this little band at the Colonial Country Club out there. We played out there, we played for the New Orleans Country Club. Metry, played, well it was in a teensy, it was a Brennan restaurant, we were in a teen, old Absent House, oh we had a lot of plays, a lot of plays.
When you played your guitar you say Walter Nelson helped you with that, taught that to you?
Yeah, Walter Nelson.
Now did you play with your same group playing guitar with that or did you play any other bands using your guitar?
Well yeah I played with several bands. I was out in the field.
Yeah that's what I wanted, some of those bands.
I played tenor banjo with George Lewis' band when Morello was sick. Oh yeah. I played a lot of jobs, George, played ghetto, lack of benefit since rock.
Oh yes, that was the mani's out of the mani's.
I played out there with George Lewis.
Did you pick up the banjo by yourself then? Or have anybody to help you on that?

Yeah a fellow that called, he was an old banjo player, a good one too. He called him Gassun but his last name was Joseph. He works for Pete Hoennman now, he don't play no more. He was a wonderful banjo player.
I've heard of him but I don't think I've heard of him.
Yeah he used to play with old man Sam Morgan. I have the picture of all the old bands.
Pictures of your band that you, or his band?
His band was playing with Sam Morgan.

When he was with Sam Morgan, I'd like to see that sometime. I'll dig it up there. Who were the best guitar players when you were young, when you were starting out? Who did you like to hear on guitar? Can you remember some of the best guitar players?

Well see for ragtime, I don't think there was nothing, nobody in town, but he was Walter. He was a little bit of a ragtime and blues player. That kind of wasn't, I don't think nobody in town before, at that time. And I liked other guitars, like Johnny St. Cyril, he was around, the time before he left, he would go up to country. Yes I knew him.
They all used to give Walter the credit.
Did you play with any other bands?
Oh yeah I played with Keita René, but not, no, not no regular, you know this, when he needed. What did you play, guitar or banjo?
Banjo. Banjo. I played with old man Chris Kelly. Who else was in Chris' band when you played with him?
Oh let's see, that was Billy Moran and us. On bass? Yeah he was bass. I was trying to think. George Boyd, he was old Clara man. You know, you haven't got that man?
I never got to meet George Boyd. Billy Moran, he was Lawrence's father? That's right.
Some relative to Lawrence.
Yeah I think he was his father. They called him Moran a lot of times, but I think his real name was Marrero, the same as Lawrence I thought. If he's the man that you mean.

This fellow here, they buried about almost a year ago, Arthur Ogans, he used to play drum. Oh yes. He was a drummer at the time. And I was on banjo, I think, on trombone. Did he have the trombone? Yeah I was trying to think really well. I can't go.
I know it's hard to remember all those names. I was pretty young man. Do you remember who else was with Kid Rene when you'd play with him sometime?
I'm trying to think now. I know one time I was playing with little Charlie, he was on drums. I was a wonderful drummer before he kind of moved in my mind.
Did his brother Joe Rene ever play with you too?

No I didn't want to think I would play with you. I was trying to think about. Did you ever do any singing in those bands? Oh no not at that time. This year lately I started. When did you start to sing about? Oh I started around about, singing around about 30, 30 now. Long and right before the war. I'll tell you all, just when I always start trying to sing is when Lurie Stahl's
strong and coming out and coming out and coming out and coming out and coming out and coming out.
I was trying to sing. I was trying to sing. I was trying to sing.
Did you ever do any singing in those bands? Oh no not at that time.
This year lately I started. When did you start to sing about? Oh I started around about, singing around about 30, 30 now.
Long and right before the war.

I'll tell you all, just when, when I always start trying to sing is when Lurie Stahl's strong and coming out with the Heavey Jeeves. Oh yeah. That was back quite, that was in the 20's. Well that's when I was trying to sing.

Way back there, yeah. Back in the 20's when he made that record. Yeah. Did you do scat singing then a good deal or did you just, or other type of songs or blues, what did you like? Noice, blues and that.
But I had other songs.
Well this bazooka that you have now, when did you make that particular instrument? We ought to get a picture of that. I guess some people have good pictures of it already.

I made that in 1924. That same one? Oh not, even the new one. I got the 1924 one on it. Oh you still have, we ought to get a picture of that. The other one I got, it's much lighter you see, and then I'm getting old you know. I got the bass made out of the new one. The old one was heavier then.

Oh it was solid brass. Yeah sure it would be. Is it much different than the tone? Oh the old one I think got a better tone. Deeper. Is it longer altogether? Shorter. Shorter. Shorter. I don't know. I don't know. But it's so heavy at the time. You don't know. I'd be playing four hours and sometimes people are like hold it up in there.
Did you ever make any other instruments, any homemade guitars or anything?
No, no. Oh I heard about it. Brennan's? Yeah, Brennan's. With the old person, they wanted the old.

Or was that the Absinthe House or Brennan's? Did they own the same places? Oh they both here own the same place but it was at the Palliot-Roll, that's his place too. Yeah that's right. That's right. That's right. What group did you have then when you made the movie?
Slow-drag I heard was playing bass, Harrison Dureck playing tenor-dang-jo, Sam Rankin playing
Or get to an album.
Have you ever worked much with the washboard bands? Any washboard bands? No. Have you ever played any jug band when you were a kid? Or tried to play the jug yourself?
No, we had contests the other year.
You never tried to play the jug band yourself? I never did. Because they got a nice tone out of some of those jugs too. I used to play those harmonicas. Well harmonica you still play it?
Well I don't think much now. I hadn't so long. I don't think I could play, the best thing I could play all night would be about one three or one.
And what year did you say you got into tuba? Around about 45.
Well before they started building those projects. Because Jim Little was staying on the back of St. Peter near Galvis. And I started on his own. Oh I see. You used his horn?
Yeah, this blowing around.
He showed me a few keys, showed me a keyboard. And you might have heard of this great tuba play, he's dead from over the river. Used to call his song. Let me see, can I call his name?
I think, did Eddie Jackson come with the most? Eddie Jackson.

That's the first. Eddie Jackson. Well before he stood my owner, how old was his. And I see he died, I bought, I don't know if it was his brother or not, there's Baptiste over there. You remember Baptiste? I think he's a drummer. Oh the drummer, yes. And his brother Mosley.
Ed Mosley. Well I bought his bass.

And I just kept the bass and kept it till I was, I would say I would I could go sick and get it and I, and after I had to go get it fixed, I thought I told him it was, it cost me more to get it better than to get a new one. More, it would be cheaper than to get a new one to fix it.
Yeah, some of those are expensive to repair.

And so I never did get a new one and one day we was playing at the fraternity house, I love you, Napoleon Abaddon Ferret. And there was a fellow, his name was, his name I think was Lanzo, Nelson Lanzo. And he was taking up law at, what's the call this university around Oldham Park?
Loyola. Loyola.

And he used to play in the band, the school band. And he asked me could I play bass too, but I told him that. He said, if you can make the scales on the bass too, I'll give you a little bit of an arm. I said, when I can come to the house, he said, it's any time to get ready. And he was staying, let's see, 42 or 7, St. George. It was between Mylon and General Perkins. And I was falling sad the morning, about half past nine. I said, he's doing now here. And I raged him, I laughed when he comes out in his room. I said, well I come with him. He said, Jesus, you don't give up a bass that he was resting. So he brought me upstairs. And I run the scales over there, it was kind of dusty. He didn't take time to wipe them up there. And he told me to take the honey, I think. And I got a jet. And Ali was Kepard using something. Oh yes, that's right, I see you.
That's the gold colored one?
Yeah, Kepard, come to it all kinds of colors.
You painted a gold, built paint on it.
Yeah, I don't know.
What bands did you play with on the street then?
Oh I was regular with Kid Howard then.
Yeah, I've heard you with Kid Howard at times.
Yeah, and sometimes Williams would use me, Abbey Williams.
Abbey, yeah.
Yeah, he'd use me when he'd ask. But I was regular with Howard.

Yeah. Haven't you got another two but now, Noon, you've got another one. Noon, you've got another two behind you now. Didn't I see you with another one a few weeks ago? Silver colored one with a hole in it or something and something falling off?
I couldn't get to, Kepard had my horn and he left that old broken horn at his house and he went off and played somewhere and I had to go play, I had to have some kind of.
That was Kepard's horn.
That was Kepard's old broken horn. He was gone with my goodness.

I was going to ask some more about any of the people in the show business. If you ever remember any of the old time vaudeville singers and comedians or any of the carnival people? You never traveled with any of the carnival shows?
I know a lot of them would come in here. You know, they haven't been in the company.

Do you remember any of the famous singers? Yeah, I don't remember. Sarah Martin. How did she sing? I never got to hear her. I think she joined church and won't sing blues. Oh, she was a mother of some songs. She was a blues musician. And Desi Smith.

I know a great comedian boy in her late years. I guess you would talk to him, Squirrel. I never did know he was writing here. He's a little short of her. Squirrel and Sweetie Walker. No, I never knew them.
I may have heard of some of those but I don't remember, I never met them. I don't think I saw them. They were from local, from here in town or did they come from out of town?

They come from out of town. Well, there was a great dancer too. Jack Wiggins. Yeah, I think I've heard of him. And the fellow, I don't know if they ever met, he used to, he was going to have a contest with Wiggins dancing. I don't know if that was his right name or his comedian named Rafford Brown. Rafford Brown. Now he danced with skate on, he skates, danced bare feet, danced with shoes on, bucks, you know, and then tap. Well, he was the fellow who wanted to challenge Wiggins.
Did you ever do any night club work with your groups? That is, aside from the traveling around the hotels, did you ever work anything on Bourbon Street or any place in that kind of area?
Yeah, Patio.
Yeah. Patio.
Patio. Well, I entertained a long time by myself at the old Absinthe House at Biennual Street.
You used just, what did you use, guitar? Guitar. Just guitar and sing.

I was waking from nine in the morning until five in the evening. And then I was over here at Lafitte Guest House with Dorothy Regal. Around eight, something, I was supposed to be at 12 or something. I'll be one, two o'clock tomorrow. Yeah. According to how my tits was coming. Yeah. And I think we could have that place shed if it didn't cause a fire to burn down.

That's the place that burned down right here at the corner. That's right. Yeah, I remember, I never did go there, but I remember once when the people told me you were working there. Must have been 15 years ago or 10 years ago. Oh yeah. A little longer there. I just remember.
I played over there so the time when Miss Mary used to have it, please. Over at the Feet's Blacksmith Shop. Yeah.
The Feet's Blacksmith Shop. Yeah. What did you use then? You used your guitar? Sometimes I was guitar, sometimes I used my group. You used your what?
The whole group of us. Oh, I see. Yeah.
Like during the holidays, they used three of us.
Yeah.
When you used three, what do you use a guitar and bass or a banjo or?
Basooka, guitar and banjo.
Yeah. Usually they don't use the string bass unless you have four of them.
Do you have any regular group? No. A standard group?
Yeah.
Who do you use?

Well, I played with, since I had bad luck and I had my house caught a fire and I lost everything I had, but I didn't get no more phone and I turned it over to the other boy that played ghetto with Miss Sam. And he had the cause out with Sam's quartet. That's how the cause was playing. I used to have the cause out with Loon's Basooka 3, I got the cause out with 68. He keeps my hand. Yeah. Does Slowdrag play with you quite a bit now?
I heard he did. Well we played, we got two jobs tomorrow night.
You see we played for Dr. Tippido and we played, that's a private house, and we played at New
Orleans Country Club.

And Dr. Tippido said he don't care what time it is if we get off of that. Did you say you were working tonight too, across the river or something? About when we were working tonight at Gentilla. Oh, Gentilla. Mm-hm.
Is that a private house party again? I think so. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
And Dr. Tippett will say he don't care what time it is we get off.
Did you say you were working tonight too across the river or something?
About, oh we're waking tonight at Gentilly. Oh Gentilly.
Is that a private house party again?
I think so.
How do you get these jobs? Do they phone you?
Yeah of course. You see what we're doing. We played last night at Metro Country Club. We played around the pool. We played three hours.
Just the three of you? Four.
Four of them. Drag was with you. Is it all a union band? I'm not trying to butt into your business and all but I just wanted they're all union members.
We couldn't use drag.
Yeah. Well are you in the union as a guitar player or a bazooka player or what kind of a player? Well a guitar player.
A guitar player.
A guitar player.

Is there anything else about your life that you'd like to tell? We've only got a couple more minutes here on the tape and if there's anything else that you could tell I think we can finish up on this reel if you've got the work then. I know you've got other things on your mind too. Anything about especially when you were young the kind of music you heard when you were a boy? Were there any other little groups around you know on unusual instruments like large board bands or tubbers or anything?

Oh yeah. Drag had a homemade bass. A fun one they called Tone Meters. That's right. I've heard you told us a little bit about that. They used to have another fellow called Lucian who played the violin. And another fellow, he was some kind of a St. Avril boy who played piano, he used to play the violin. He was well at St. Avril. What a lot of that man back.
Oh yeah I heard it again, I never got there.

And violin, guitar, a fellow called Freddie Gould, I believe he was living somewhere in Alton town. He was a wonderful old time guitar picker. And Freddie Gould and slow drag, Lucian on violin. Willis St. Diego played the violin. And Freddie Gould played the guitar. Well one other question too about nowadays of course the little kids, you didn't take up music until you were about fourteen you say.
That's right.
But I wondered even younger kids like the shoeshine boys now, you know they get together and they

play. And they play. And they play. And they play. And they play. And they play. And they play. And they play. And they play. And they play. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. On a fence, yeah. And we tighten and we get music from there.
Like a harp, huh?
Yeah, come on down to the side.
Yeah, and a little sharp ones up to the longest. Yeah, beat it with sticks. Like a piano or a harp?

Yeah, big plant-nice music. I don't think I'm about to forget. In fact, there ain't no weather there, I don't think that. I don't think I forgot. I think I can make a big piece of it. So you beat on them with sticks? A little, little stick. Take your knife and kill a little stick.
Yeah, pretty good. I'd like to hear that. Oh, it was something I was told. Yeah, I bet that was that. You did that too and all the kids?
Well, they had a fellow they called, Edward Rose and I believe. He was an older fellow. He was the first one we saw down there. Yeah.

Were there any groups that the kids had to go around on the street? So I wondered, you know, like on Mardi Gras Day or different things, or at night time, you know, to try to play for the tourists or anything.

Yeah, that's how I used to, I got many women for that, like Mardi Gras Day, just run away from home, because my mother didn't want to go and I used to get, but ladies and Mardi Gras then sometimes I used to dance and dress, you know, and spread around the street. And I used to play at home on it and they'd give us two bits a piece. Yeah. You see, all the ladies would put up for two bits a piece. That's pretty good. And that was that two was getting a dime piece, but that was for the musicians. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
